chicken-thigh-sauteed-skin-not-eaten.title: Chicken thigh, sauteed, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh without skin is the meat from the bird's thigh, cooked by sautéing in a pan. Removing the skin reduces fat content while preserving the juiciness and characteristic flavor of the meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thigh meat contains more iron and zinc than chicken breast.
When sautéed without skin, some fat melts away, making the dish less caloric but still flavorful thanks to Maillard reactions.
Chicken thigh is a staple in many world cuisines – from French coq au vin to Asian teriyaki dishes.
Thigh meat is more tender than breast due to higher connective tissue content.
Proper high‑heat sautéing can create a crisp exterior without excess oil.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides high‑quality complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune health, metabolism, and skin integrity.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Removing the skin dramatically cuts saturated fat, making it more suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Contains creatine
items.content: Creatine aids cellular energy production in muscles, beneficial for active individuals.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 165 °F (74 °C).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some people are allergic to chicken proteins and may experience reactions.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: If the thighs are marinated, sodium levels can be high, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Histamine formation
items.content: Improper storage can lead to histamine buildup, causing food intolerance symptoms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless chicken thighs can be sautéed, braised, baked, or added to salads and soups. Pat the pieces dry before cooking to achieve a golden crust. Serve with vegetables, whole grains, or your favorite sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw thighs refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days, or freeze in airtight bags for up to 6 months. Cooked meat lasts 3‑4 days in the fridge. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

fish-salmon-baked-or-broiled-coated.title: Fish, salmon, baked or broiled, coated

content.title: About
content.content: Salmon is a marine fish from the Salmonidae family, prized for its delicate flavor and high content of healthy fats. When baked or broiled with a coating, it stays juicy while the crispy crust adds a pleasant texture contrast.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salmon can migrate between the ocean and freshwater rivers where they spawn.
Coatings are often made from whole grains, spices, and a small amount of oil, enhancing aroma and crunch.
Baking retains more omega‑3 fatty acids than deep‑frying in oil.
In Japan, salmon is sometimes served as “sabai,” lightly seared and brushed with soy sauce.
Salmon is called the “king of fish” because of its high vitamin D content.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s support heart health, reduce inflammation, and aid brain function.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Salmon provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B12 and B6 help form red blood cells and maintain nervous system health.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Regulates calcium levels and supports the immune system.

items.title: Selenium
items.content: An antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including salmon.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: While salmon generally has low mercury, pregnant women and children should limit intake.

items.title: High‑salt coating
items.content: Overly salty coatings can raise blood pressure; choose low‑sodium options when possible.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Coating and oil increase the dish’s calories, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coated salmon can be served as a main dish with vegetable sides, mashed potatoes, or a fresh salad. It also works well sliced for sandwiches, salads, or tossed with pasta.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared product refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 63 °C before serving.

stewed-chicken-with-tomato-based-sauce-m.title: Stewed chicken with tomato-based sauce, Mexican style

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed chicken in a Mexican‑style tomato sauce is made from bite‑size pieces of chicken breast or thigh, slowly simmered in a fragrant blend of tomatoes, chilies, onion, garlic and spices (cumin, oregano, coriander). The dish has a rich, mildly spicy flavor with a hint of acidity and the characteristic aroma of Mexican cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mexican tomato sauces often include fresh chilies, giving the dish its signature heat.
Chicken is traditionally marinated in lime juice before cooking to keep the meat tender.
The stew is commonly served with corn tortillas, rice, or beans.
Mexican cooking relies heavily on aromatic herbs and spices such as cumin and coriander to boost flavor.
Slow‑cooking helps retain most of the nutrients in both the meat and the sauce.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken contains B3 (niacin) and B6, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Lycopene in tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may help protect cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Beneficial minerals
items.content: The dish supplies potassium, magnesium and iron, important for muscle function and blood health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with skinless chicken and minimal oil, the stew remains relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: Spice level
items.content: The chilies can be too hot for people with sensitive stomachs or gastritis.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Using canned tomato paste or broth can raise the sodium level of the sauce.

items.title: Undercooking risk
items.content: Chicken should reach an internal temperature of 75 °C to prevent salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stew hot, typically with corn or flour tortillas, rice, beans, or a fresh salad. Optional toppings include avocado, sour cream, or shredded cheese for a milder taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze for up to 2 months after cooling to room temperature.
